title: Witches and Neighbours: The Social and Cultural Context of European Witchcraft
author: Robin Briggs
publisher: HarperCollins (1st ed. 1996); Penguin (paperback ed. 1997); Blackwell (2nd ed. 2002)
subject_focus: Social-cultural analysis of European witch prosecution with particular depth on Lorraine archival records, arguing that witch accusation was embedded in ordinary community social relations and that no single explanatory model adequately captures its complexity.
summary: Witches and Neighbours is Briggs's synthesis of the European witch-trial historiography, combining broad comparative analysis with deep archival work on Lorraine witch prosecution records from the Archives Départementales de Meurthe-et-Moselle. The book's central argument is against monocausal explanation: neither the Thomas-Macfarlane charity-refusal model, nor Karlsen's property-inheritance model, nor feminist misogyny explanations, nor political conspiracy theories account for the diversity and complexity of actual accusation patterns as revealed in systematic archival research. Briggs found that Lorraine witch accusations arose from multiple community tensions simultaneously — economic disputes, sexual rivalry, property conflicts, personal enmity, physical misfortune — and that their victims were far more socially diverse than simpler models predicted, including a notably higher proportion of male accused than English studies had suggested.
scholarly_significance:
Witches and Neighbours is the most comprehensive scholarly synthesis of European witch-trial historiography available in English and the most detailed study of any Continental European prosecution jurisdiction. Its contributions are both empirical (the Lorraine archival data) and analytical (the explicit critique of dominant theoretical frameworks).

  The Lorraine findings specifically complicate several established models. The proportion of male accused (approximately 25-30% in Lorraine versus approximately 8-12% in Essex) challenges the English pattern's universalization. The diversity of accusation dynamics — charity-refusal patterns coexisting with other patterns in the same archive — challenges the charity-refusal model's claim to primary explanatory status. The community-level variation within a single jurisdiction challenges any explanation that locates the driving force primarily in institutional or ideological factors.

  Briggs's explicit engagement with and critique of Ginzburg, Thomas, Macfarlane, Karlsen, and others makes the book an essential methodological reference for understanding the state of the historiographic debates at the end of the twentieth century.

key_arguments.claim: Witch accusation was not adequately explained by any single causal model (charity refusal, property inheritance, misogyny, demonological ideology, state-building) because actual accusation patterns were too diverse, too locally variable, and too multiply-determined to conform to single-factor explanations.

key_arguments.concept: Lorraine as paradigm case for European diversity
key_arguments.claim: Lorraine accusation patterns differed from English patterns in proportions of male accused, accusation dynamics, and social profiles of accusers and accused — demonstrating that European witch prosecution cannot be modeled on English evidence alone.

Witch accusation was primarily generated by ordinary community social tensions — disputes over property, reputation, economic transactions, sexual relations — that already existed independently of demonological ideology and that the witch accusation framework provided a mechanism for processing.

relation_to_database: Referenced in the lorraine-ducal-court inquisitorial_body entry, the men-accused-of-witchcraft persecuted_group entry, and as methodological counterpoint to the simpler models in the widows-early-modern and elderly-women-accused entries. Briggs provides the primary evidence for Lorraine prosecution patterns.
scholarly_disagreement: Briggs's anti-theoretical pluralism has been criticized for lacking explanatory leverage — showing that accusation dynamics were diverse doesn't help explain why they occurred. Feminist critics have argued that Briggs understates the misogynistic dimension even where it's not the exclusive explanation. Ginzburg's microhistorical approach and Briggs's archival sociology are methodologically incompatible in ways that neither has explicitly resolved.
source_method: Published text, HarperCollins 1996; based on Archives Départementales de Meurthe-et-Moselle records
